summary: A practical, intermediate-level guide to writing faster SQL by understanding how the database engine actually executes queries. The lesson starts with the four phases of query execution and the central role of the cost-based optimiser, whose plan quality depends on the cardinality estimates it derives from collected statistics. It then walks through reading an execution plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE in PostgreSQL (and equivalents in SQL Server, MySQL, Oracle), covering the most common node types — sequential scans, index scans, index-only scans, bitmap scans, and nested loop, hash, and merge joins — and the technique of comparing estimated and actual row counts to find where the planner's model diverges from reality. Index design is treated at length: B-tree mechanics, the importance of selectivity, the leftmost prefix rule for composite indexes, equality-before-range column ordering, covering indexes with the INCLUDE clause to enable index-only scans, and the real maintenance cost of every additional index. A dedicated section catalogues the anti-patterns that silently defeat indexes — SELECT *, functions on indexed columns, implicit type conversions, leading wildcards in LIKE, OR across unrelated columns, and the NULL pitfall in NOT IN — with the canonical rewrites for each. The lesson then covers manual subquery-to-join rewriting (IN vs EXISTS semi-joins, decorrelating correlated subqueries into grouped LEFT JOINs), keeping statistics fresh and handling column correlation with multi-column stats, and three structural optimisations that matter once queries are individually reasonable: keyset pagination instead of OFFSET (which gives 10–100x speedups on deep pages), batching writes (multi-row inserts, single-transaction batches, prepared statements, COPY/BULK INSERT), and the three layers of caching (buffer pool, plan cache, application-level). It closes with a six-step optimisation loop — measure, get the plan, find the largest estimate-vs-actual gap, diagnose the cause, change one thing, re-measure — applied to the small number of queries that dominate the workload.
